passage:
“Pranav, no! Gentle hands,” said Ishita.
Pranav had shoved Dev off the sandpit edge because Dev had taken the yellow truck. He stood red-faced, fists clenched, shouting “Mine!”
“You're angry. That's your truck, and Dev took it.” She held his hands. “But pushing hurts. Use your words: ‘Mine, please.’”
“Mine puh.”
“Good. Dev, can you give it back?”
Dev handed it over, and Pranav took it, then patted Dev's arm, unsure.
“Gentle,” Ishita said. “Like that.”

qa.q: Why did Pranav push Dev?
qa.a: Because Dev had taken the yellow truck.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he pushed Dev, and what was he missing?
qa.a: He felt angry and strongly wanted his truck, and he did not yet have words to say “no” or “mine” calmly. It was not cruelty.

qa.q: What could Ishita do next time to prevent a push?
qa.a: She could stay near, step in early to help the children take turns and remind Pranav of his words.

qa.q: How might Dev feel after being pushed?
qa.a: He may feel startled and hurt, so a gentle pat from Pranav helps him feel safe again.

grounding: A toddler pushes when frustrated and lacks words, and an adult sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches gentle hands.

passage: Toddler room note, Thursday. When Bilal took the wooden blocks Parveen was stacking, Parveen, two, hit his arm with her open hand and shouted, then grabbed the block back. I moved close, crouched and said, “You wanted your blocks. You were cross. But no hitting.” I held her hand and stroked it gently on Bilal's arm: “Gentle.” Then I gave Bilal his own blocks. Parveen watched, calmer. I will keep this calm approach and model gentle touch. 🙂 Imran

qa.q: What did Parveen hit Bilal for?
qa.a: Because he took the blocks she was stacking.

qa.q: What does Parveen's hitting show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows anger and a strong wish to keep her blocks, since she did not have words for “no” or “mine”. It was not meant to be cruel.

qa.q: What worked well in how Imran handled the incident?
qa.a: Imran stayed calm, named her feeling, set a firm limit and showed gentle touch, then made sure Bilal had his own blocks.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel after the incident?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and sore, and Imran's attention shows him he will be looked after.

grounding: A toddler hits when frustrated and lacks words, and the teacher sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches gentle hands.

passage:
In the courtyard of their village house, Devika's cousin grabbed her little cloth ball. Devika screamed, shoved him, and then hit his arm.
Manjula, her mother, came over quickly and calmly, holding Devika's hand. "You're angry. He took your ball. I won't let you hit." She stroked the cousin's arm softly with Devika's hand. "Gentle hands. Say, 'Mine.'"
Devika glared, then said, "Mine!" The cousin handed the ball back.

qa.q: What did Devika's cousin grab?
qa.a: Her little cloth ball.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she shoved and hit her cousin?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated that her ball was taken, and she didn't yet have the words to say so.

qa.q: What made Manjula's response wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, stopped the hitting, named the anger, showed gentle hands and gave Devika a word to use.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Devika says "Mine!"?
qa.a: The cousin may feel a bit surprised, but hearing the word makes it clearer and easier to give the ball back.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's hitting with calm limits, a named feeling, gentle hands and a word to use.

passage:
In the sandpit at a Dublin park, a boy took Liam's red spade. Liam pushed him hard, and the boy sat down in the sand.
Freya, Liam's mother, knelt between them. She held Liam's hands firmly, not roughly. "You're cross. You wanted your spade. I won't let you push." She turned to the boy. "Are you okay?"
Then to Liam: "Say, 'My turn.'"
"My tun!" Liam shouted. The boy held out the spade.

qa.q: What colour was Liam's spade?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he pushed the boy?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated that his spade was taken, and he had no words ready to say so.

qa.q: What did Freya do well?
qa.a: She held his hands firmly but calmly, named his feeling, checked on the other boy and gave Liam words to use instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might the boy experience being pushed?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and hurt, and Freya's check helped him feel noticed.

grounding: A toddler pushes when his toy is taken, and his mother sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches words.

passage: I'm Rafiq, from the flat opposite, and I was at their door on Friday when it happened. Asif's mother took a pair of scissors away from him, and he hit her arm, hard, screaming. I expected her to shout. She didn't. She caught his hand and held it. "You're angry. You wanted those. I won't let you hit." He kicked and cried. She waited, holding on. After a bit, he slumped against her.

qa.q: What did Asif's mother take away from him?
qa.a: A pair of scissors.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he hit his mother's arm?
qa.a: He was probably angry and frustrated at losing the scissors, not trying to be cruel; slumping against her later suggests he was worn out and needed comfort.

qa.q: Which of the mother's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm, holding his hand and naming the feeling worked, because it set a limit without adding more anger.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see the mother's reaction?
qa.a: Rafiq is surprised, having expected shouting, and seems impressed by her calm.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler hit in frustration and his mother answer with a calm limit and named feeling.

passage:
Monday. Cousin Arun took Ganga's spoon. She smacked his arm, hard.
Karthik knelt and held her hand gently. “You're angry. He took your spoon. I won't let you hit.” He gave the spoon back.
Thursday. Arun grabbed her ball. Ganga shoved him. Karthik caught her hands. “Angry? Say ‘mine.’”
The next Tuesday, Arun reached for her doll. Ganga's hand went up, stopped, and came down in a pat. “Mine!” she shouted. Karthik grinned.

qa.q: What did Arun take from Ganga on Monday?
qa.a: Arun took Ganga's spoon.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she smacked and shoved Arun?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated that her things were taken, and without many words, hitting and pushing were how the strong wish came out.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that worked over the days?
qa.a: He calmly stopped the hitting, named her anger and gave her a word, "mine," so she could learn gentler hands.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Ganga pats instead of hits?
qa.a: He would feel proud and pleased, which is why he grinned.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler hitting and pushing when frustrated and an adult using calm limits, naming the feeling and teaching gentle hands.
